title: I have not heard (Avot 5:7)
hookLine: seven marks of the wise: don't interrupt, answer in order, and say "I haven't heard" when you haven't
tomorrow: which is better: a short fuse, or a fast cool-down?

cards: Some apps will invent a whole answer, sources and all, rather than leave a blank. People do it too. The nod in class.
The oh yeah, totally, about a show you never watched. The confident guess in a meeting, because a blank can look like losing. And once you bluff, you have to keep bluffing.
So what do the wise say when they just don't know? Avot has three words for it, and they're on a list of seven.

teach.b: Avot 5:7 sets two people side by side: the golem and the wise. Golem here isn't a clay monster. It means unformed, a lump not yet shaped.
The wise one has seven marks. Doesn't speak first in front of someone wiser. Doesn't cut into a friend's words.
Isn't rushed to answer. Asks to the point, and answers to the point. Takes first things first and last things last.
Says of what they haven't heard, I have not heard. And admits the truth. The golem does the reverse of each.
Notice how ordinary the list is. Nothing about being brilliant. Every mark is about how you hold what you know, and what you don't.
And look at the exact phrase. Not I don't know: I have not heard. It names where knowing comes from.
Someone taught it to you, or no one has yet. The Talmud says Rabbi Eliezer never said a thing he hadn't heard from his teacher. That's not timid; it's careful with the chain.
So, for this week, when a question lands and you're blank: three words, and a door left open. Not heard, yet.
Then a question back: tell me.
The blank stops being a loss and becomes the start of a lesson.

how: In traditional Torah study, saying 'I have not heard' or 'I don't know' is part of the give-and-take; students are taught to name who taught them a teaching and to admit what they haven't learned.

games.q: what does “i have not heard” mean?
o: refusing to listen to gossip or rumors
a vow of silence kept during study

games.q: the seven marks — tap the pairs.

s: in Avot 5:7, golem means a clay monster
here it means an unformed person, the opposite of the wise.
not interrupting is one of the marks of the wise
the wise one doesn't cut into a friend's words.

games.q: at work, your manager asks what you thought of a report you never got. everyone turns to you. what does Avot's wise one say?
o: 'I haven't seen that one yet. Can you send it?'
nod, say it looked solid, and read it after the meeting.
talk about the parts of the project you do know well.
games.why: the wise one says 'I have not heard' about what they haven't heard, and asks to the point. the blank stays honest, and the door stays open.

practice: Think of a moment coming up where someone might ask you something you can't answer: a class, a meeting, a dinner table. See the pull to bluff arrive, and let it pass.
Then say the words you'll use instead, quietly, once: I haven't heard that; tell me.

wordCard.voice: I have not heard: one of the seven marks of the wise in Avot 5:7. Honest about the chain, and open to more.

orig.note: Hebrew: I have not heard, a mark of the wise in Avot 5:7.

carryVoice: Three words to keep handy: I have not heard, then tell me. Until next time.
